rows.timeline_year_basis: The Qur'an is never dated; it is the single starting block
rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Explicit: 2:283 provides for a pledge (rahn) held as security when no scribe can record a debt on a journey.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: 'If you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then a pledge in hand' — the one contract of the ten with a verse that names it. Tafsir on this verse (Tabari, Qurtubi) reads the pledge as security for debt. Why here: The Qur'an opens the Rahn ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 2:283.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2068
rows.detail: The Prophet bought food grains from a Jewish merchant on credit and mortgaged his iron armor — the living rahn precedent.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Aisha. What: Aisha's narration: the Prophet's own armor pledged for barley. The same narration anchors credit purchase (and qard); Bukhari's pledge chapters build on it. Graded Sahih. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “We mentioned about pledging in Salam trade to Ibrahim, Aswad, with reference to Hadrat Aishah , narrated a Hadith to me: The Prophet (ﷺ) purchased food grains from a Jew on credit and mortgaged his iron armor to him.” It stands in Sales and Trade. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2068.

rows.name: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1214
rows.detail: Ibn Abbas: the Prophet died while his armour was pawned for twenty sa' of food for his family.
rows.detail_long: Who: Jami' al-Tirmidhi is the collection of Muhammad al-Tirmidhi (824-892), a scholar of the hadith sciences known as a master of hadith analysis. Narrator: Ibn Abbas. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library, from Tirmidhi's Business chapters with his own grading preserved ('This Hadith is Hasan Sahih'): the pledge outstanding at the Prophet's death — rahn practised to the very end, for household provisions. The strongest possible endorsement-by-practice of secured debt. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Narrated Ibn 'Abbas: The Prophet (ﷺ) died while his armour was pawned for twenty Sa' of food that he got for his family. [Abu 'Eisa said:] This Hadith is Hasan Sahih.” It stands in The Book on Business. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1214, Book on Business.

rows.detail: Thirty sa' of barley, dated. 'Aishah: when the Messenger of Allah died, his armour was mortgaged with a Jew for thirty sa' of barley.
rows.detail_long: Who: Riyad as-Salihin is a hadith collection by al-Nawawi (1233-1277), the Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. Narrator: 'Aishah. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: the pledge quantified (thirty sa' of barley) and the creditor identified across religious lines — rahn as an ordinary, cross-communal credit instrument in Madinah. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “When Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died, his armour was mortgaged with a Jew for thirty Sa' (measures) of barley..” It stands in The Book of Miscellany. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Riyad as-Salihin 1720.

rows.name: Bulugh al-Maram 985
rows.detail: Usufruct of the pledge for its upkeep. The pledged animal may be ridden, its milk drunk — by whoever bears its upkeep. Benefit follows expense, even inside a pledge.
rows.detail_long: Who: Bulugh al-Maram is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: Abu Hurairah. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: 'An animal may be ridden, due to what is spent on it, when it is in pledge; and the milk of a camel may be drunk, due to what is spent on it... the responsibility of spending on it is upon the one who rides and drinks.' The pledge is not sterile: whoever maintains the collateral takes its usufruct — the maintenance-benefit symmetry classical rahn law builds on. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: "An animal may be ridden, due to what is spent on it, when it is in pledge; and the milk of a camel may be drunk, due to what is spent on it, when it is in pledge. And the responsibility of spending on it is upon the one who rides (it) and drinks (its milk)." .” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Bulugh al-Maram 985.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed gloss on 2:283: on a journey with no scribe, 'let the creditor take from the indebted person a security for his loan' — and trust without security binds the debtor's conscience.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas on 2:283: the pledge-in-hand substitutes for the written record when writing is unavailable; and where a loan is extended on pure trust, the trusted party must 'deliver up that which is entrusted to him' and fear Allah in repayment. Security and conscience presented as the verse's two enforcement tracks. Attribution traditional, not critical — hence 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q2:283.

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir on 2:283: the pledge stands in for the missing scribe — citing Ibn Abbas: even a scribe without paper, ink or pen triggers it.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Kathir (1301-1373) of Damascus was a Qur'an commentator, historian and scholar, an expert in tafsir, history and fiqh. A Shafi'i, he is known for a commentary that takes a critical approach to Isra'iliyyat (stories taken from earlier communities). What: Ibn Kathir on 2:283: travel plus deferred debt plus no scribe = 'let there be a pledge taken (mortgaging) given to the creditor'; and Ibn Abbas widens the trigger — 'even if they find a scribe, but did not find paper, ink or pen'. The pledge as the documentation-substitute, its scope read generously. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Rahn ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1373 (year of the author's death). Source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q2:283.

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail: Al-Tabari on 2:283: the pledge as security and the trustee's duty.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari (839-923) was a Sunni scholar, historian, jurist and Qur'an commentator from Amol in Tabaristan who worked in Baghdad. He followed the Shafi'i school for nearly a decade, then developed his own school of law (the Jariri school), which lasted about two centuries after him. He is best known for his Qur'an commentary, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan), and his historical chronicle. What: His long treatment of 2:283 covers the pledge-in-hand rule and the discharge of trusts. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 923 (year of the author's death). Source: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q2:283.

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi's massive ahkam treatment of 2:283 — the fullest verse-level law of pledge.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Qurtubi (1214-1273) was an Andalusian Maliki jurist and Qur'an commentator, taught by the scholars of Cordoba; after the city fell in 1236 he moved to Egypt. His twenty-volume commentary, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qurtubi), is a general commentary written from a Maliki point of view. What: His 2:283 commentary is effectively a pledge treatise: conditions, possession, use of the pledged asset. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Rahn ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1273 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q2:283.

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Al-Mughni's Kitab al-Rahn sets the Hanbali pledge rules; all four schools accept rahn.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: Possession, custody, whose risk, and whether the creditor may use the pledged asset — the standard classical questions, answered per school. In the work itself (vol. and page 4:245; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And rahn (pledge) in the Law: the wealth that is made a security for the debt, so that it [the debt] may be taken in full from its price if taking it in full from the one who owes it is not possible. And it is permissible, by the Book and the Sunna and consensus.” It also states: “Rahn in the language: fixedness and continuance. It is said: 'rahin' water, that is, still.” It also states: “As for the Book, it is the saying of God, exalted is He: {and if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then pledges taken in hand} [al-Baqara: 283].” It also states: “And as for the Sunna, 'A'isha - may God be pleased with her - narrated "that the Messenger of God - may God bless him and grant him peace - bought food from a Jew, and pledged to him his coat of mail." Agreed upon.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Rahn ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mughni.

rows.name: Imam Malik ibn Anas
rows.detail: Malik relates 'The pledge given as security is not forfeited', and holds that a condition handing the pledge to the creditor if payment is late is void.
rows.detail_long: Who: Malik ibn Anas (711-795), called the Imam of Medina, is the eponym of the Maliki school, one of the four Sunni schools of law; the school became the norm in much of North Africa and al-Andalus. Al-Muwatta is his work. Al-Shafi'i was his best-known student. What: Muwatta 36.10 'Prohibition against Forfeiting Pledges Given on Security' (no. 13): Malik says of the forfeiture condition, 'I think that the time condition is void.' Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Rahn ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 795 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Muwatta, Book 36 (Judgements), section 36.10.

rows.name: Yahya ibn Sharif al-Nawawi
rows.detail: Al-Nawawi: a pledge 'cannot be legally given except by mutual consent of the parties interested, i.e. by offer and acceptance'.
rows.detail_long: Who: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (1233-1277), known as Muhyi al-Din, was a Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. His works include Minhaj al-Talibin and Riyad al-Salihin; al-Asnawi described him as the editor and refiner of the Shafi'i school. What: The standard Shafi'i manual opens its book of rahn with offer and acceptance as the basis of the pledge. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Rahn ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1277 (year of the author's death). Source: Minhaj al-Talibin, Book 11 (Pledge or Security).

rows.timeline_year_basis: SS39 adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 23, Bahrain, 15-17 Rabi' I 1430 / 12-15 March 2009
rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.work_title: Shari'ah Standard No. 39 (Mortgage and Its Contemporary Applications)
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 39 (2009) codifies rahn for modern use: mortgaging shares, sukuk, investment accounts, income streams and insured assets.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS39 modernizes the pledge: what may be mortgaged (including fungibles, units, accounts), mortgage of income yet to be owned, insurance of the pledged asset, and the creditor's rights — the standard behind today's Islamic collateral packages and ar-rahnu schemes. Adopted 12-15 March 2009 (meeting 23, Bahrain). This also closes the earlier gap where Rahn had no confirmed dedicated standard. Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1/1 the mortgage binds the mortgagor once concluded; only the mortgagee may revoke; 3/2/1 the mortgaged asset must be Shari'ah-permissible, well specified and deliverable; 3/3/1 the secured debt must itself be permissible (sale income, guarantee, salam or istisna'a commodity, owed usufruct); 3/4/1 on default the mortgagee may claim sale of the asset — any surplus after the debt returns to the mortgagor; 4/3 interest-based bonds, preference shares and the like may not be mortgaged. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Rahn ladder; shown at 2009 (SS39 adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 23, Bahrain, 15-17 Rabi' I 1430 / 12-15 March 2009). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 39 (2009).
